replying_to: Replying to Scale-Invariant Teaching for Semi-Supervised Object Detection
display_title: Official Review of Paper2382 by Reviewer d1ou

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes improvements for Semi-Supervised Object Detection (SS-OD) methods. The authors suggest to use three mechanisms to extend current SS-OD frameworks. Specifically, they extend UBT (Liu et al., 2021) with three main contributions:

1. They suggest to downsample the weakly augmented image by the same ratio of downscaled FPN levels. Then run inference on both the strongly augmented image and downsized image by the student. Finally, they apply consistency loss between the corresponding FPN layers of images inferred in the different scales. The loss used is the KL loss between the class probabilities, and L2 for the box regression,
 
2. They use soft labels from the teacher similar to Humble Teacher (Tang et al., 2021). The authors claim that differently from the Humble Teacher work, they balance the background and foreground labels with the following gradient balancing mechanism. Another difference is that they do not ensemble the teacher model predictions.

3. They use a mechanism to balance the gradients from easy and hard examples inspired by the work of Gradient Harmonizing Mechanism (Li et al., 2019). They use this mechanism only for classification of the unlabeled objects. This mechanism is similar to Focal-Loss work and aims to tackle the inherent foreground-background class imbalance in object detection.

The method presented is comprised of a single stage training - a single training phase for both the labeled and unlabeled data with two branches, one for each type of data.

The authors conducted experiments on Faster-RCNN with Res50 + FPN backbone.
content.main_review:
### strengths

The authors present novel scale-invariance consistency loss for semi-supervised object detection. This component alone improves the 10% labeled data scenario by about 3 mAP on COCO (23.86- > 26.80). With the additional soft-labels from Humble Teacher (Tang et al., 2021) and Gradient Harmonizing Mechanism (Li et al., 2019) they surpass the current SOTA by a margin (5%-> +2.6, 10%-> +3.5, 100%->+1.2).

The authors shares important experimental details such as the update and lr decaying strategy for the EMA teacher model. 

### weaknesses

The documentation of experiments and method explanation need to be improved. For example:
- Section 1 Paragraph 2: _"Fig. 1a, the standard variance of the scale of instances in MS-COCO is 188.4, while that of ImageNet is 56.7"_ what is the unit of measure? Also, the images were resized differently therefore the statistics are incomparable.
- Section 3.1 _"Towards handling the large scale variation, the s is selected from {1, 2, 3, 4}, which also matches the sizes of feature maps in FPN and the label assignment rules"_ . It is not clear if the method uniformly samples from the set {1,2,3,4} or that a single number is used.  Later, in sec 4.3 it says that s=2 is the optimal scale. It is not clear which value was used for the experiments in table 1.
- Section 4.2  _"Fig. 1c shows that the discordance between different sizes is alleviated"_ the setup is not clear, was it measured during the training phase? or did you augment the validation images to measure the discrepancy.
- Section 4.3 _"Fig. 5 shows that the fraction of valid instances..."_ the term "valid instances" was not defined. It seems like an important and critical quantity that was not defined explained or further discussed.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The ideas and presented in the paper are novel and present a decent improvement on current art with supportive experimentation. The paper present both novel and incremental improvements for extending current SS-OD approaches.
However, the writing; method details; documentation and explanations need to be improved as was detailed in main review.

content.title: Response to reviewer d1ou
content.comment:
Q1: "Fig. 1a, the standard variance of the scale of instances in MS-COCO is 188.4, while that of ImageNet is 56.7" what is the unit of measure? Also, the images were resized differently therefore the statistics are incomparable.

A1: The unit of standard variance is pixel. For the ImageNet classification task, images are typically resized to 224 * 224 for training. Enlarging the image size does not improve the test accuracy significantly.(e.g., Swin-B 224 * 224 has 83.5 top-1 accuracy, while Swin-B 384 * 384 has 84.5 top-1 accuracy.) However, the detector is typically trained with a large input size, such as 1333 * 800, to get a superior result. Training with too small input size may lead to an inferior result for Faster-RCNN on the COCO dataset.  

So we discuss the typical (empirical optimal) training input size for ImageNet classification and COCO detection task. Under this setting, the classification model is supposed to handle a small scale variation (56.7), and the detector model is supposed to handle a large scale variation (188.4). Hence, we believe that the statistics are comparable.


Q2: It is not clear if the method uniformly samples from the set {1,2,3,4} or that a single number is used. Later, in sec 4.3 it says that s=2 is the optimal scale. It is not clear which value was used for the experiments in table 1.

A2: We would like to revise the description to make it clear. "Towards handling the large scale variation, the s is uniformly selected from {1, 2, 3, 4}, which also matches the sizes of feature maps in FPN and the label assignment rules." For the claim in Sec 4.3, the model achieves the best result on the COCO dataset when the downsampling rate is set to 2. (i.e., when s is set to 1.). Downsampling ratio $r = \frac{1}{2^s}$. We would like to revise the notation to be consistent across the paper and thanks for your constructive suggestion.


Q3: "Fig. 1c shows that the discordance between different sizes is alleviated" the setup is not clear, was it measured during the training phase? or did you augment the validation images to measure the discrepancy.

A3: The distribution is measured after the training phase. We augment the validation images to measure the discrepancy. We would like to add the setup into the caption to make it clear.


Q4: Fig. 5 shows that the fraction of valid instances..." the term "valid instances" was not defined. It seems like an important and critical quantity that was not defined explained or further discussed.

A4: As described in Sec 4.3, the detector is trained to detect object instances in a particular scale range, according to the anchor matching rule. (e.g. the Faster-RCNN constrains the valid detection scale range, from 22.6 to 724.1, theoretically.) Therefore, only the instances in the above scale range are effective during the training and testing phases. If the downsampling ratio (i.e. the $s$ in Q2.) is too large, most instances are out of the valid scale range and do not contribute to training the detector. Hence, we set the downsampling ratio to 2 (i.e. s is set to 1).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a new semi-supervised method that addresses the problems of existing self-training based methods. It comes with three key components: scale consistency regularization, weight consistency regularization with soft target and re-weighting strategy.
content.main_review:
Strengths
- The proposed semi-supervised method tries to address different problems via different strategies at the same time. Scale consistency regularization plays an important role in detecting objects with different scales. Using soft targets instead of hard targets makes is threshold free and simple to apply.
- The experimental settings are well designed and results are well oraganized.

Weaknesses
- In the Introduction section, it says that the scale of objects varies smaller for classification tasks than object detection. This is true for some datasets, e.g. ImageNet and COCO. However, this is not a valid statement. We can still perform (multi-label) classification tasks on detection datasets. Thus scale invariance is also equally important for classification. It'll be interesting to see if the same scale invariance teaching can benefit classification tasks (at least some analysis).
- The writing needs some improvement. 
- Notations needs to be defined before using. For example, SUP in Table 2, Baseline in Table 3.
- Re-weighting strategy is used for dealing with class imbalance. However, the paper does not compare it with other methods to show the efficacy of the proposed method.
- No geometric augmentations are used in all experiments. It'll be interesting to see how such augmentations can affect the performance.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method works well but the novelty is not high enough. It also needs some improvement in both writing and analysis.

content.title: Response to reviewer 2dFM
content.comment:
About the Novelty:
Our contribution is to solve the large scale variance, False Negative samples and inferior localization precision problem which is challenging and meaningful in semi-superivsed object detection task and may be further extended to other dense prediction tasks. It is the first time that the scale consistency regularization is introduced to Semi-Supervised Object Detection. Although the implementation details are simple, the improvement is significant. We believe that solving the existing problems is also important.

Q1: It is not a valid statement that the scale of objects varies smaller for classification tasks than object detection. This is true for some datasets, e.g. ImageNet and COCO.

A1:  We agree with the reviewer's suggestion. We would like reclaim that "The scale of objects varies in a small range for ImageNet-1K classification dataset, whereas the scale variation is large across object instances in MS-COCO dataset." 

Q2: Scale invariance is also equally important for classification. It'll be interesting to see if the same scale invariance teaching can benefit classification tasks (at least some analysis).

A2: We believe that Scale invariance is also equally crucial for classification. Recently, the model pretrained with some self-supervised learning methods, such as SwAV[1] and SimCLR[2], outperforms the previous SOTA semi-supervised classification methods. SwAV sets the cluster of the large-size crop as the target of small-size crops, which is also a kind of scale invariance regularization. This scale consistency regularization can be extended to other self-supervised methods. As shown in the following table, SWAV and other self-supervised methods also benefit from scale invariance.

| DeepCluster-v2 [1] | 70.2   |      74.3          |   
| SwAV [1] | 70.1   |       74.1          |   

[1] Unsupervised Learning of Visual Features by Contrasting Cluster Assignments, NIPS 2020.
[2] A simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations, ICML 2020.
[3] Self-labelling via simultaneous clustering and representation learning, ICLR 2020.

Q3: Compare Re-weighting strategy with other methods to show the efficacy of the proposed method.

A3: We conduct experiments by replacing our re-weighting strategy with OHEM (Online Hard Example Mining) and Focal Loss. Baseline is training without any class balancing technique. The result shows that our method is effective. (Results on MSCOCO 2017 val. All the model is trained with 10% labeled coco train dataset.)

display_title: Official Review of Paper2382 by Reviewer Juqd

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposed a method for the semi-supervised object detection task. The authors proposed a method that compromises several (relatively small) changes compared to the existing work: (1) leveraging the fact that we have multiple-scale features in the FPN and enforce consistency regularization between features across scales, (2) using soft pseudo-labels instead of hard pseudo-labels, and (3) re-weight the KL Divergence by the sample numbers (Sec. 3.3, inspired by an existing work). Combining these key changes, the authors demonstrate SoTA performance across existing benchmark datasets (though missing some experimental settings).
content.main_review:
**[Pros]**
- comprehensive ablation study on the proposed method showing how each component impact the model's performance
- The proposed method is simple 

**[Cons]** 
- I am slightly concerned about the novelty of the proposed method in leveraging scale-invariant features.  While this has not been done before for semi-supervised object detection, it's not a surprise method and its performance improvement is somewhat expected. I think this could be a paper for a performance-targeted conference, but probably not to the standard of an ICLR paper. 
- I am not sure if the proposed method can be easily extended to other detectors (see comments below)

**[Questions]** 
- The authors claim that the proposed scale_invariant consistency regularization method can be easily extended to other detectors. While the authors use FPN as an example to illustrate the proposed method in Sec. 3.1, it's not clear to me if the same method can be easily extended to other detectors, e.g., SSD, YOLO, DETR, etc.
- In Sec. 3.2, what exactly is the weight consistency regularization? From the equation (3) and the description in Sec. 3.2, it reads like the traditional consistency loss, but instead of using hard pseudo-labels like the one in Unbiased Teacher, the authors proposed to use soft pseudo-labels. They also use MSE for regression loss, which is pretty common for applying consistency regularization for regression tasks. 
- In Table 2, is there a particular reason why the authors decided to not compare the performance when data percent is at 0.5 or 1%?

**[Minor comments]**
- "weight consistency regularization for aligning the name of the unsupervised loss". Is this a typo for using "name" in this sentence? 
- "which doesn't torture the geometric information". I am not sure if I understand this sentence. Did the author mean to say "contain the geometric information"?
- In Table 2, when Data percent is 100%, UBT's "Iter" should be 270k instead of 360k.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the amount of performance improvement as well as the technical novelty of the work, I am rating this work as "marginally below the acceptance threshold". The main two concerns for me are (1) the novelty of the method and (2) whether if we can actually easily adapt the proposed method to other object detectors.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2382 by Reviewer Juqd

content.title: Response to reviewer Juqd
content.comment:
About the Novelty:
Our contribution is to solve the large scale variance, False Negative samples and inferior localization precision problem which is challenging and meaningful in semi-superivsed object detection task and may be further extended to other dense prediction tasks. It is the first time that the scale consistency regularization is introduced to Semi-Supervised Object Detection. Although the implementation details are simple, the improvement is significant. We believe that solving the existing problems is also important.

Q1: Novelty of scale consistency regularization.
A1: To the best of our knowledge, it's the first time that scale consistency regularization is brought to semi-supervised object detection task. An object detector is supposed to output consistently for an image in different sizes. However, we observe a discrepancy in the objectness scores, as indicated in Fig.1c. The ratio of foreground anchor to background anchor increases as the score distance becomes large, implying that **the baseline model detects an object instance in the image while is blind to the instance in a different size, in the case of a significant objectness score distance.** This inconsistency is typically alleviated by the multi-scale inference ensemble, which increases the computational cost and requires complicated operations to fuse the bounding boxes. **Detector trained with our scale consistency regularization is more scale-invariant than the baseline model.** As shown in Tab.5, the gain of multi-scale testing is less for our method than the baseline. Fig.1c also demonstrates that the scale distance between the prediction of an image in different sizes is less than the baseline model. **Scale consistency regularization is an implicit ensemble method that is completed during training**. Compared with multi-scale testing, **our scale consistency regularization improves performance while not requiring an additional computational cost.**

Q2: It's not clear to me if the same method can be easily extended to other detectors.
A2: Most detectors (e.g. RetinaNet, Faster-RCNN) assign foreground labels to the "anchor box" according to a similar rule, the Intersection-over-Union (IoU) threshold criterion. For DETR, a single feature map detector, we match the predictions of input in different views according to Hungarian algorithm, where the pair-wise matching cost is defined as:
$L_\text{match} = D_\text{JS}(p_1, p_2)  +\lambda L_\text{IoU}(b_1,b_2)$,
where $D_\text{JS}(p_1, p_2)$ is JS-Divergence between the probability vectors and $L_\text{IoU}$ is GIoU loss[1].
According to the above analysis, our method can be extended to RetinaNet and DETR with different backbones. The results in the following table demonstrate that our method is valid for different classes of the detector.
 
According to the above analysis, our method can be extended to RetinaNet and DETR with different backbones, the results is shown in the following table. (Results on MSCOCO 2017 val. All the model is trained with 10% labeled coco train dataset.)

| Detector   |      RetinaNet  w R50 |  RetinaNet  w R18   | DETR w R50   |
|----------|:-------------:| :-------------:| :-------------:|
| Baseline | 23.6  |       21.5          |     64.9          |
| Ours | 33.0  |       31.4          |       69.3         |

For RetinaNet, the experiments are conducted on MS-COCO set with 10\% labeled training data. Due to the extremely long training epoch of DETR, we report the result on Pascal VOC 2007 test set. Both supervised and our DETR are trained for 300 epochs.


Q3: What exactly is the weight consistency regularization?
A3: Our weight consistency regularization is designed to alleviate the noise problem which arises from the False Negative samples and inaccurate bounding box regression, as indicated in Fig.1b. This regularization is also a self-distillation framework with mutual learning mechanism. The slowly progressing teacher generate soft pseudo-labels for unlabeled data in an online manner. Therefore, the teacher and student jointly learn to improve each other. The soft target and regression prediction of weak augmented input are labelled for the student model.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2382 by Reviewer TME4

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Scale-Invariant Teaching approach for semi-supervised object detection. More specifically, the proposed approach enforces consistency between predictions from different image scales, uses soft labels w/ re-weighting to avoid false negatives and balance positive and negative examples, and uses exponential moving average to update the teacher model. Experiments on PASCAL VOC and COCO show that the proposed approach obtains very promising semi-supervised object detection results.
content.main_review:
**Strengths**
1. The proposed re-weighting strategy is interesting.
2. The proposed approach obtains promising results.

**Weaknesses**
1. Novelty.
The novelty of the proposed approach is limited. 1) It's not new to use soft labels and exponential moving average for semi-supervised object detection (Tang et al., 2021) (Liu et al., 2021). 2) The proposed scale consistency can be seen as another kind of strong augmentation to train the student model. In addition, it's not new to enforce consistency between different image scales for object detection w/ limited labels [a] (although the techinical details of how to do scale consistency are not exactly the same).
2. Experiments. 
This paper needs more experiments to show the effectiveness of the proposed approach. 1) It would be interesting to show the results of removing the proposed scale consistency approach and adding image scaling as a kind of strong augmentation for student model training. 2) It would be interesting to show results of more object detections (like RetinaNet (Lin et al., 2017b), DETR [b], Deformable DETR [c], etc.) with more CNN backbones (like ResNeXt w/ and w/o deformable convolution).

[a] Comprehensive Attention Self-Distillation for Weakly-Supervised Object Detection

[b] End-to-End Object Detection with Transformers

[c] Deformable Transformers for End-to-End Object Detection
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, as stated in **Weaknesses** in the **Main Review** part, the novelty of the proposed approach is limited and more experiments are needed. Therefore, I would like to give a weak reject to this paper.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2382 by Reviewer TME4

content.title: Response to reviewer TME4
content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate your constructive suggestion. In this paper, we focus on the challenge of semi-supervised object detection. We first **analyze the large scale variance, massive False Negative samples and class imbalance problem existing in current arts. The analysis is well-supported by experimental result (e.g. Fig.1 and 4).** Then we propose scale consistency regularization and reweight strategy to solve the problems. 

About the Novelty:
Our contribution is to solve the large scale variance, False Negative samples and inferior localization precision problem which is challenging and meaningful in semi-superivsed object detection task and may be further extended to other dense prediction tasks. It is the first time that the scale consistency regularization is introduced to Semi-Supervised Object Detection. Although the implementation details are simple, the improvement is significant. We believe that solving the existing problems is also important.


Q1: Novelty of soft target.
A1: The pioneer distillation (soft target) is first proposed by [1, 2] to improve the performance of a  compact ‘student’ deep neural network. Although the improvement from distillation on the image classification is significant, **these methods cannot be directly extended to the detection task which is supposed to handle large variance of object sizes and class imbalance**. Some works [3,4,5] contribute to solving the class imbalance problem in detection distillation task. **To alleviate the class imbalance problem, (Tang et al., 2021) simply selects top-K proposals as soft targets, which requires carefully selected hyperparameter, while we set all anchor boxes and proposals as soft targets in a hyperparameter-free manner.** Furthermore, the weighting consistency regularization benefits from our reweighting strategy. Our weighting consistency regularization aims to **alleviate the noise incurred by the False Positive sample and the inaccurate bounding box, while (Tang et al., 2021) adopts soft target to distill much richer information from the teacher**, compared to sparsely hard-selected high-confident pseudo ground truths in the existing work. We believe that **our explanation and motivation is more convincing and well-supported** by our experimental results and Fig.1b. Besides, **we do not ensemble the teacher model predictions.**

Q2: The proposed scale consistency can be seen as another kind of strong augmentation to train the student model. The novelty of scale consistency regularization.
A2: The proposed scale consistency regularization is more than large scale jittering augmentation. The object of our method is $L = L(x) + L(x') +L_\text{scr}(x, x')$, while the object of a large scale jittering augmentation is $L =  L(x) + L(x')$, where $x$ and $x'$ are the input image in different views. The $L_\text{scr}$ is the scale consistency loss. The constraint of our method is stronger than large scale jittering augmentation. Thus we believe that the parameter space of local minimum is a subset of that of large scale jittering. The following table also shows that our method encourages the model to converge with less generalization error. (Results on MSCOCO 2017 val. All the model is trained with 10% labeled coco train dataset.)

| Scale Jittering Range   |      [640, 800]     | [300, 1200] | Ours [640, 800] |
|----------|:-------------:| :-------------:|:-------------:|
| Result | 31.4  |       32.0             |            34.0 |

An object detector is supposed to output consistently for an image in different sizes. However, directly optimizing model without scale consistency regularization can not result in a scale-invariant object detector, as illustrated in Fig.1c. We observe a discrepancy in the objectness scores, as indicated in Fig.1c. The ratio of foreground anchor to background anchor increases as the score distance becomes large, which implies that **the baseline model detects an object instance in the image while is blind to the instance in a different size, in the case of a significant objectness score distance.**


Detector trained with our scale consistency regularization is more scale-invariant. As shown in Tab.5, the gain of multi-scale testing is less for our method than the baseline. Fig.1c also dementrates that the scale distance between the prediction of an image in different sizes is less than baseline model. **Scale consistency regularization is an implicit ensemble method which is completed during training**.


Together with the other proposed components, our method surpasses the current state-of-the-art methods. [6] focuses on the attention map and ensemble the attention map of different transformations, however, ensemble prediction leads to an inferior result in semi-supervised object detection, as shown in (Tang et al., 2021).
